# 0 What Pragmatism Means

- [dangling] "The pragmatic method in such cases is to try to interpret each notion…": "such cases" and "each notion" resolve through the preceding statement, which has the list of notions, so this passes.
- [dangling] "What difference would it practically make to anyone if this notion rather than that notion were true?": "this notion… that notion" refers to the notions in the earlier statements, so it resolves and passes.
- [dangling] "Which party is right depends on…": "Which party" has no antecedent. The statement comes after the squirrel dispute, but the note never says there were two sides. The sentence is a question fragment, and "party" is not introduced.
- [dangling] "If you mean passing from the north of him…": "him" is the squirrel, which an earlier statement names, so this passes.
- [cut lost content] "The corpus of a ferocious metaphysical dispute was a squirrel…": the quotes are stitched from two source locations ("The corpus of" + "a ferocious metaphysical dispute"). Between them the source reads "The corpus of the dispute was a squirrel", and "ferocious metaphysical" actually comes from the prior sentence. The statement reads like a clean sentence, but the joined quote is a spliced rewrite.
- [dangling] "The corpus of a ferocious metaphysical dispute…": nothing in the note identifies who disputed or where. The statement does not read as an opening, but "a" makes it self-contained, so it passes.
- [cut lost content] "Which party is right depends on what you PRACTICALLY MEAN…": the trimmed words are the speaker's framing ('"Which party is right," I said, "'). Only stance was dropped, so this passes on cuts.
- [reworded] "The corpus of a ferocious metaphysical dispute was a squirrel…": "the dispute" is rewritten as "a ferocious metaphysical dispute" using words from a different source sentence, which is a reword rather than a trim.
- [weak] "This human witness tries to get sight of the squirrel…": "This human witness" refers to the human being in the preceding statement. It resolves, so it passes. Support is fine.
- [dangling] "You are both right and both wrong…": "both" has no named parties in the note, because no earlier statement introduces two sides. It is dangling.

Counts: pass 14 / weak 1 / fail 0 / dangling 2 / outside-frame 0
